I farm 18 mu here in Quzhou County, ten mu in wheat-maize rotation and the rest in vegetables. Ten years of doing this has taught me that saving money on fertilizer is the fastest way to lose money on yield. I watch what the big growers west of my village do, and I do the same or a little more. A bad harvest means borrowing from relatives; wasting half a bag of urea is just a cost I can absorb.

My wheat is already in the ground from last October on ten mu. I plant improved seeds from the county seed station — not the most expensive kind, but the ones that Lao Zhang across the road gets good results with. Last year I got about 500 kg per mu. This year I will put down the same fertilizer: base dressing of about 40 jin of compound fertilizer per mu when I planted, then top-dress with urea twice — 30 jin per mu at green-up and 20 jin per mu at heading. That works out to about 25 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus 8 kg phosphorus and 6 kg potassium. I will irrigate four times from my well: winter water, green-up water, jointing water, and grain-filling water. I will spray pesticide twice — once for weeds, once for aphids when it warms up. The field was rotary-tilled before planting last fall.

After wheat harvest in early June, I will plant hybrid maize, Zhengdan 958, direct into the stubble without tilling — saves time and keeps the moisture. Everyone around here does no-till now. Maize gets about 22 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. I will water three times and spray three times for armyworm and weeds. I expect 600 kg per mu if the rain cooperates.

My four mu of autumn cabbage is my cash crop. I use hybrid F1 seeds because the heads are tight and heavy. Cabbage needs more food than grain — I will put down 24 kg nitrogen, 10 kg phosphorus, and 12 kg potassium per mu, half as base and half top-dressed. I will irrigate six times; cabbage leaves wilt fast and never recover if they dry out. I will spray five times — the cabbage butterflies will strip it bare if you miss even one week. Rotary-tilled deep. I expect about 4,000 kg per mu.

On three mu of eggplant, I buy seedlings from the nursery in town in April. Eggplant needs potassium to set fruit, so I give it more than cabbage — 26 kg nitrogen, 10 kg phosphorus, and 15 kg potassium per mu. Seven irrigations, six pesticide sprays. Rotary-tilled and plastic-mulched. Yield should be around 3,200 kg per mu.

My one mu of stevia is a side plot the buyer comes to collect. I will give it 12 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 8 kg potassium per mu, water four times, and spray twice for insects. Rotary-tilled. Should get about 800 kg of fresh leaves per mu.

I wanted to cut back on fertilizer last year because the price went up, but my husband said no — we tried that three years ago on eggplant and lost a third of the crop. Now I buy what I bought last year, plus a little extra urea for the wheat because the green-up looks a bit pale compared to my neighbor's field.

decision.reasoning_summary: I manage 18 mu by rotating wheat and maize on 10 mu while dedicating 4 mu to autumn cabbage, 3 mu to summer eggplant, and 1 mu to stevia. I base every decision on last year’s practice, neighbor observations, and a strong bias toward applying enough fertilizer to protect yield rather than risking a thin crop. With primary schooling and ten years of hands-on experience, I think in bags and jin, follow successful neighbors, and adjust upward only when I see greener fields around me. My well supports regular irrigation, and on this large farm I can absorb some input costs, but a harvest failure is still a disaster I avoid by sticking to what has worked before.
